title: Balloon Vine: How to Stop This Climbing Weed in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Balloon Vine in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Balloon vine, or parol parolan, climbs over palay in rainfed fields. Learn to spot its lantern shaped fruits and pull it before it smothers your rice.
excerpt: Balloon vine is a climbing broadleaf weed that grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Its papery, lantern shaped fruits make it easy to recognize, but by then it may already be climbing your crop. This page shows how to spot it early and how to remove it before it covers your palay.

heroImage.alt: Balloon vine (Cardiospermum halicacabum), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: H. Zell, CC BY SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This vine belongs to the soapberry family, the same family as rambutan and lychee. Farmers know it by many names: alalayon, bangkolon, lubo lobohan, parol parolan, paltu paltukan, parya aso and paspalya. Names like parol parolan and lubo lobohan point to its fruit, which looks like a small lantern or balloon. Balloon vine grows in rainfed lowland rice fields.

As an annual, it lives for one season and spreads by seed. Its long stems climb by wrapping thin tendrils around anything nearby, rice stems included. Each balloon shaped fruit holds a few round black seeds, and each seed carries a small white spot shaped like a heart. When the papery fruits dry and split, the seeds drop into the field for the next crop.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about balloon vine
rows: Alalayon, bangkolon, lubo lobohan, parol parolan, paltu paltukan, parya aso, paspalya

blocks.text: Look for a thin vine with long, slightly hairy stems that climbs over the rice or nearby plants. The leaves grow one at a time along the stem on slender stalks. Each leaf splits into three, and each of those parts splits into three again, so you see many small leaflets with toothed, sometimes lobed edges. Like other broadleaf weeds, it has netted veins. Tiny white flowers come first, then the papery, lantern shaped fruits.

items: Thin vines climbing up and over rice plants, using small curling tendrils to hold on.
Long, slightly hairy stems that tangle between the rice hills.
Leaves divided into three, then three again, with toothed, sometimes lobed leaflets.
Very small white flowers that you can easily miss among the leaves.
Papery, green, lantern shaped fruits that puff up like little balloons.

blocks.text:
Balloon vine competes with your palay for light, water and fertilizer, but its climbing habit makes it worse than most broadleaf weeds. Its stems wrap around rice tillers and spread a layer of leaves over the crop. That shade slows the rice below. Heavy vines can also pull rice stems down, which makes harvest harder and can spoil grain that touches wet ground.

Its dry fruits and seeds can also get mixed into the harvest. Besides that, tangled vines give rats and insects cover inside the crop. Since it climbs, the longer you wait, the harder it gets to pull out without breaking the rice.

items: Cut and pull the vine while it is still small, before it climbs the rice. Unwind it gently so you do not break the tillers.
Remove plants before the lantern shaped fruits dry and split, and carry them out of the field in a sack.
Clear the vine from fences, levees and nearby bushes too, since plants there can drop seed into the paddy.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold balloon vine down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Balloon Vine Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Balloon Vine?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Balloon Vine

items.q: What is balloon vine called in Tagalog?
items.a: Many farmers call it parol parolan or lubo lobohan, names that point to its lantern or balloon shaped fruit. In other areas you may hear alalayon, bangkolon, paltu paltukan, parya aso or paspalya. Whatever you call it, the papery fruit and the climbing stems make it easy to know in the field.

items.q: How do I control this vine in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first, so keep the levees and field edges clean. Then cut and pull young vines before they climb the rice, and remove them before the fruits dry. If you need a herbicide, choose one made for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label, since a wrong spray can hurt the palay it climbs on.

items.q: Why should I pull a vine that looks so harmless?
items.a: Because it does not stay small. It climbs, spreads its leaves over the rice and shades the crop. Its weight can also pull rice stems down before harvest. On top of that, each fruit drops seeds that sprout next season. Pulling it early, before it climbs and fruits, saves you work and protects your palay.
